summary: Describes an experimental LDAP referral service run by the OpenLDAP Project that generates referrals from service location information published in DNS SRV records. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: This is a sign-post service that tells you which directory server to ask by looking up clues in the Internet's address book.

questions: ldap referrals from dns srv records
how to locate ldap servers with dns
subtitle: An LDAP referral service that uses DNS to locate directory servers.

tldr.problem: LDAP directory services were hard to discover globally without complex registration infrastructure, and most LDAP implementations didn't support automatic service location.
tldr.mechanism: The OpenLDAP Root Service maps LDAP distinguished names to domain names and uses DNS SRV records to find LDAP servers for each domain, then returns referrals to those servers.
tldr.outcome: This experimental service shows how DNS can glue together a global LDAP directory without requiring protocol-specific registration infrastructure, allowing anyone with a domain name to participate in a distributed directory.

today: RFC 3088 is an Experimental protocol. The OpenLDAP Root Service was run as an experiment by the OpenLDAP Project but has never become a standard. Modern LDAP implementations have better service discovery mechanisms, and the lack of security features made it unsuitable for production use.

sections.title: What the OpenLDAP Root Service Does
sections.content:
The OpenLDAP Root Service is an experimental referral service that helps LDAP clients find the right directory server. LDAP is a protocol for accessing directory services, which store information about people, organizations, and resources in a hierarchical structure called a distinguished name (DN).

Most LDAP servers support generating referrals, which tell a client to ask a different server instead. The OpenLDAP Root Service acts as a root referral server that other LDAP servers can point to when they do not have information locally. The service automatically generates correct referrals by consulting the Domain Name System (DNS).
sections.eli5: This is a sign-post service. When you ask it a question about a directory, it does not answer; instead it points you to the right directory server by looking up the answer in the Internet's address book.

sections.title: Mapping Names to Domains
sections.content:
To find the right server for a DN, the service must first convert it to a domain name. An LDAP DN like UID=jdoe,DC=example,DC=net contains domain components (the DC= parts) that map directly to a domain name. The service reads these components left to right and concatenates them with dots to form example.net.

If a DN contains non-domain attributes (like CN=Jane Doe,O=example,C=US), the service cannot map it to a domain, so it returns an error. This preserves the link between LDAP naming and DNS naming, allowing the system to leverage existing DNS infrastructure.
sections.eli5: The address format tells the service which domain to look up. If it cannot figure out the domain from the address, it gives up.

sections.title: Using DNS SRV Records to Locate Servers
sections.content:
Once the service has a domain name like example.net, it queries DNS for service records (SRV records) at _ldap._tcp.example.net. These records are a standard way to publish the location of services. Each SRV record returned contains a hostname and port where an LDAP server listens.

If the DNS query returns no records or if any DNS error occurs, the service returns an error to the client. It does not currently use the priority or weight information in SRV records; future versions may optimize the selection of servers based on these hints.
sections.eli5: It asks DNS where LDAP servers live for that domain. If DNS knows the answer, the service passes it back as a referral.

sections.title: How Clients Use the Service
sections.content:
LDAP clients connect to the service at ldap://root.openldap.org:389 and submit requests for entries. When the service receives a search or other operation, it tries to map the target DN to a domain and find servers as described above. It returns the LDAP URLs for those servers as a referral.

The service accepts only anonymous binds (login without credentials) to keep it simple and avoid privacy concerns. It is read-only; all operations either return referrals or errors. Other LDAP servers can be configured to use this service as a superior referral, allowing a hierarchical directory where the local server refers unknown entries to the root service.
sections.eli5: You ask the service a question in LDAP format. It either tells you where to find the answer or tells you it does not know.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
The service returns information derived from public DNS, so it has no special security model. It accepts only anonymous clients and provides no encryption, making it vulnerable to eavesdropping and DNS spoofing attacks. The IESG note observes that without encryption, session integrity, or authentication, an attacker could intercept or forge responses.

The service also has no protection against denial-of-service attacks and can be blocked by malicious DNS responses. The RFC states that future versions should support encryption via Start TLS, DNSSEC for integrity verification, and other hardening measures. The simplicity is intentional for an experimental system, but the lack of security makes it unsuitable for sensitive operations.
sections.eli5: Because this is experimental, it skips the security protections that a real directory would need. Anyone listening can see your requests, and a person could trick it into giving wrong answers.
